items.title: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)
items.text: Date: 2026-10-09 Author: Codebot Topic: opencode, task-plugin, handoff, instructions, naming, npm, github, release
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 1. Objective (or: A Five-Second Fix and a Much Longer Conversation)
items.text:
Part 2 ended with the plugin happily named, close_task live, and a REST-ful future ahead of it. This part is quieter on the surface and does two unrelated things:

  1. Fix a single sentence inside the tasks tool - a pointer that told the agent what to do, was quoted back to the user as if it were a pleasantry, and never got obeyed.
  2. Audit the plugin for a public release (npm + GitHub) and settle its name - which turns out to be the same naming question Part 2 declared closed.

Nothing was published, renamed, or deleted. This is the session where the instruction learned to give orders and the plugin learned what it would have to fix before strangers see it.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 2. Background (or: The Tool That Will Not Let You Start Cold)
items.text:
The plugin owns ~/.opencode/plan/: active/TASK-*.md, an archive/, a canonical session-index.json, and a session-handoff.md that records what the last session established. Four tools wrap it - tasks (list), task_new, verify, close_task (archive).

The vocabulary has been layered since the V1 era, and it is worth restating because it drove the decision in section 4.5:

Altitude Name What it is Store plan the one directory, ~/.opencode/plan Unit task a TASK-*.md file State todos the checkboxes inside a task

So: plan -> task -> todos. The path says plan, the files say TASK-, and the tools say task. That is not drift; it is two altitudes of the same idea.

The tasks tool is special because it is the first thing a fresh session reaches for, and a bare list of files is dangerous - a task list without context reads as "this is all you need to know", which is how three stale copies of the handoff once survived three syncs while the tool reported a healthy list. So tasks prints a bounded excerpt of session-handoff.md ahead of the list, plus a pointer to the full file. That pointer is the sentence this session fixed.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 3. Problem (or: The Instruction Read Aloud Instead of Followed)
items.text:
A fresh session ran tasks. The output ended with:

## Session Handoff (read this before the task list)

**Date:** 2026-10-09 (from file mtime; no **Date:** line in the handoff)

...

Full narrative: /home/sigit/.opencode/plan/session-handoff.md - read it before
acting on the tasks below; it records what the last session established,
including corrections to earlier claims.

The agent then did the one thing the sentence did not want: it relayed the sentence. "Read session-handoff.md before acting on tasks" appeared in the reply as advice, and the task list was presented - without the file ever being opened. The user noticed before the damage did:

You said Read .../session-handoff.md before acting on tasks but you didn't read it for me.

The user's second point was sharper still: the line was treated as prose. It looked like narration, it sat inside a block of narration, and it was addressed to no one in particular. So it was quoted. Which is a different failure from being ignored - the reader engaged with the text and still did not act on it.

The second thread of the session is the plugin itself. It works, it is not polished, and its author wants it public via GitHub plus npm. What follows in section 4.3 is what "not polished" means when you actually look.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 4. Work Performed (or: Orders Instead of Description)
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 4.1 Rewrite the pointer as an imperative
items.text:
The fix was three edits in task-manager.ts, all of them wording. The header became an order with an addressee:

- ## Session Handoff (read this before the task list)
+ ## Session Handoff - AGENT ACTION REQUIRED: read the handoff file (path below)
+ before you present the task list

The pointer stopped describing and started instructing, and it named the failure mode out loud:

- Full narrative: <path> - read it before acting on the tasks below; it records
- what the last session established, including corrections to earlier claims.
+ Full narrative: <path>
+ AGENT INSTRUCTION (not for the user): before outputting the task list below,
+ use the read tool on that path and act on what it says. It records what the
+ last session established, including corrections to earlier claims. Relaying
+ this pointer to the user instead of reading the file does not comply.

Three properties did the work:

  • An addressee. "Agent instruction (not for the user)" removes the ambiguity that made the old line quotable.
  • An order before the list. The read is demanded before the task list is shown, matching the output order the tool controls.
  • The anti-pattern named. Calling out "relaying this pointer does not comply" closes exactly the loophole that was used.

The third edit was documentation, in this file's own house style: a paragraph in the function's WHY comment recording the 2026-10-09 incident, so a future "cleanup" of that wording knows it is load-bearing. The convention in this codebase is that every non-obvious choice carries its reason next to it.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 4.2 Rebuild and verify the artifact, not the exit code
items.text:
npm run build (tsc) exited clean, which - per the lesson this series keeps re-learning - is not proof. The proof was grepping the compiled output:

dist/task-manager.js:497: "## Session Handoff - AGENT ACTION REQUIRED: ..."
dist/task-manager.js:527: `AGENT INSTRUCTION (not for the user): ...`

The new wording is in the file that actually loads. The plugin is loaded at session start, so the change takes effect next session; inside the same session the old wording is still in memory.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 4.3 The publish-readiness audit (or: Five Things Between Here and Public)
items.text:
A public release means strangers add this plugin to their config. That reframes every local shortcut as a defect. The audit found five, plus two curiosities:

# Finding Why it blocks public use 1 package.json declares "dependencies": {} while the lockfile's root records @opencode/plugin@2.0.16 Manifest and lock disagree; npm ci fails and the package declares no dependency it needs 2 No README.md and no LICENSE file (the field says MIT; the file does not exist) GitHub front page is empty; license is a promise without a document 3 Bundled skills leak personal infrastructure skills/session-close/SKILL.md names homelab:/srv/repo/opencode-v2/tasks.git, ~/.opencode/bin/sync-plan.sh, and the mem0 store layout; the plugin copies skills/* into every installer's global skills dir 4 The plugin silently runs git pull/commit/push origin main on tool calls pullTasks() is called from listTasks(); a stranger's plan dir may not be a git repo, or may have a different remote 5 Hard-coded store path ~/.opencode/plan plus the hard-coded sync Fine for this author, surprising for everyone else a Hub config uses the field plugin (singular); V2 docs document plugins It works today; unresolved whether plugin is an alias or a legacy key b ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json loads bare names like opencode-task-plugin Worth documenting the exact install shape so others reproduce it

Finding 3 is the one with actual blast radius. A plugin that distributes your ops runbooks - complete with your homelab hostnames - into every user's skills directory is not a public plugin yet; it is a leak with a plugin attached.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 4.4 Name availability (or: The Catchy Name Was Taken by a Stranger)
items.text:
The author's working title was "OpenCode Plan Manager". It is catchy. It is also taken, twice, by the same person:

Probe Result npm opencode-plan-manager TAKEN - v1.1.11, "A plugin for managing plans in OpenCode" GitHub yurihbm/opencode-plan-manager EXISTS - "tools for better plan management by AI agents", since 2026-02-08 npm opencode-task-plugin free (registry 404) npm opencode-planmanager free npm opencode-plan-manager-plugin free GitHub thsigit/opencode-task-plugin free (git protocol check; see section 8 for the method)

A direct-collision namespace is worse than an ugly name. Sharing an exact name with a competing plugin means mutual confusion in every search result, issue tracker, and "which one did you mean" conversation, forever. The interesting outcome of the check was not the availability table, though; it was the decision.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 4.5 The decision (or: Part 2 Was Right the First Time)
items.text:
The author's mental model, restated in the session, decided it:

I prefer to work on one task file/dir at a time... Thus, we were using ~/.opencode/plan but keep the name task. To keep using name task, the mental model is plan -> task -> todos.

That model makes "Plan Manager" the right outer name - the product manages the plan store - while task stays the right tool-level word. The two are not in conflict; they are two altitudes. So the resolution is layered, not split:

  • Package/repo/plugin id: keep opencode-task-plugin (no rename).
  • README title: "OpenCode Plan Manager" - the catchy brand, carried by the front page rather than the package name.
  • Tagline / early section: teach plan -> task -> todos, including the V1-to-V2 store migration that explains why files say TASK- inside a plan/ directory.
  • npm description + keywords: carry plan, todos, agent so search finds it despite the package id saying only "task".

Part 2 declared the naming closed at opencode-task-plugin; this session proposed re-opening it and then re-closed it, for a better reason. Naming is done when the cost of changing it exceeds the confusion it removes. With an exact-phrase collision already on the board, it does.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 4.6 Accounts and the handle hunt
items.text:
Publishing needs two logins and one handle:

  • gh is installed but not authenticated; npm whoami returns ENEEDAUTH. Both logins are interactive and user-only.
  • The git identity is sigit <sigit@localhost> - an email that maps to no GitHub account by name. The handle was recovered by searching GitHub commits authored by the git email: thsigit, 313 commits, repos including nix-journal and opencode-google-workspace.
  • The npm username was declared as thsigit. Its existence is not machine-verifiable (the registry user endpoint returns 405; the maintainer search shows zero packages, which is what a fresh account looks like). Login will settle it.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 4.7 The plan, written down
items.text:
All of it went into a task file rather than staying in chat - TASK-publish-plan-manager-plugin-to-npm-and-github.md, sixteen checkboxes over five phases (accounts, manifest fixes, content, repo+CI, publish+verify), with the audit findings, the availability table, and the naming rationale recorded. Two boxes are done (name, handle); the rest wait on a "go".

The only deliberate scope change: the plugin's implicit git sync ships gated off. The code stays, the behaviour is wrapped in an option defaulting to false, and nothing pushes until it is explicitly asked to. Local consequence accepted and recorded: this author's own instance stops auto-syncing too, and their explicit sync-plan.sh is unaffected.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 5. Diagnosis (or: Why Prose Gets Quoted)
items.text:
The wording bug is a small, generalizable finding about instructions embedded in tool output:

Text addressed to no one gets relayed, not obeyed. The old line was grammatically an instruction and socially a description. It sat in a block of narration ("Most recent session recorded:", "Full narrative: - it records..."), so its genre was summary, not command. A reader - human or agent - scans for genre first and content second. The fix was not emphasis; it was changing the genre: name the addressee, state the action, and name the failure mode.

The failure is not "ignored", it is "quoted". An ignored instruction produces no engagement. Here the agent engaged with the text enough to surface it - in the wrong channel. That is why the anti-pattern clause matters: telling the reader that relaying is not complying removes the satisfying-but-wrong action.

A tool that prints instructions owns their wording. tasks could instead just read the handoff itself, but the design deliberately does not (a handoff can run to tens of KB and tasks is called often). Given the choice, the excerpt has to be an order, because it is the only part of the file the agent sees by default.

This is the same shape as a lesson this series already carries - verify the artifact, not the exit code - one level up. There, a clean exit did not mean the job ran. Here, a present instruction did not mean it was followed. Both are cases of "the observable said one thing, the intent was another."
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 6. Preliminary Assessment
items.text:
The instrument is fixed and verified in the compiled artifact; it will take effect next session. The publish project is fully planned, partially unblocked (name and handle resolved), and deliberately not started. Nothing was published, renamed, or deleted.

The audit is the more valuable output. It converts "this plugin works" into a concrete list of what "public" additionally requires: a declared dependency, a README, a LICENSE file, scrubbed skills, and a sync path that does not fire implicitly. Four of those are mechanical. The fifth - the skills scrub - is the one that stops a personal homelab from shipping inside a stranger's config.

One thing this session did not do: re-test the fixed wording by calling tasks again in a fresh process. That is by design (the plugin loads at session start), and it is the first item of the next session's verification.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 7. Solution Summary
items.text: Concern Before After Handoff header "Session Handoff (read this before the task list)" "Session Handoff - AGENT ACTION REQUIRED: read the handoff file ... before you present the task list" Handoff pointer descriptive prose to a generic reader imperative addressed to the agent, with the failure mode named Why-comment silent records the 2026-10-09 quote-instead-of-obey incident Plugin name opencode-task-plugin opencode-task-plugin (proposed "Plan Manager", rejected on collision + vocabulary) Public brand - README title "OpenCode Plan Manager", tagline plan -> task -> todos Git sync implicit pull/commit/push on tool calls to be gated behind options.sync, default false Release plan in conversation TASK-publish-plan-manager-plugin-to-npm-and-github.md, 5 phases Published - nothing (no npm publish, no repo, no rename)
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 8. Verification (or: What Was Actually Proven)
items.text:
Claim Evidence The wording change is in the compiled artifact dist/task-manager.js:497 and :527 carry the new strings after npm run build The old wording was quotable prose reproduced in the session: the pointer appeared in an agent reply with the file unopened npm opencode-plan-manager is taken registry returns v1.1.11; description "A plugin for managing plans in OpenCode" GitHub yurihbm/opencode-plan-manager exists commit/search results; unrelated same-named repo by moondrop12138 also appears thsigit/opencode-task-plugin is free git ls-remote (auth prompt = absent) with thsigit/nix-journal as a positive control; REST API was rate-limited (403) Handle is thsigit GitHub commit search on the git email: 313 commits, nix-journal, opencode-google-workspace Not logged in to either registry gh auth status = not logged in; npm whoami = ENEEDAUTH The plugin's dependency graph is inconsistent package.json dependencies: {} vs lockfile root @opencode/plugin@2.0.16 Bundled skills name personal infrastructure grep of skills/ for hostnames and personal paths

Unproven and stated as such: npm username thsigit existence (405 on the user endpoint; zero maintainer packages), and the plugin-vs-plugins config field question (it loads today; the reason is unresolved).
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 9. Pending Actions
items.text:
All publish work is planned and none of it executed. The task file carries the checklist; in brief:

  1. Phase 0: gh auth login, npm login (interactive, user-only).
  2. Phase 2: declare @opencode/plugin and regenerate the lock; set version 0.1.0; gate the git sync behind options.sync (default false); add prepublishOnly: tsc.
  3. Phase 3: README (title "OpenCode Plan Manager", plan -> task -> todos section), LICENSE file, genericize the two bundled skills, .gitignore (keep dist/ committed).
  4. Phase 4: git init, GitHub Action (npm ci && npm run build).
  5. Phase 5: npm pack review, publish 0.1.0, create thsigit/opencode-task-plugin, clean-room install test.
  6. Next session, first thing: call tasks in a fresh process and confirm the new wording shows and is obeyed.
path: The Instruction That Got Quoted (or: Preparing the Task Plugin to Go Public)

items.title: 10. Recommendations (or: Make the Output Give Orders)
items.text:
Instructions embedded in tool output must be imperatives with an addressee. "The X is at " is documentation. "Read before you show the list; relaying this line does not comply" is an instruction. If a tool depends on the reader doing something, write it the second way - genre before emphasis.

Name the failure mode, not just the goal. Telling the reader what not to do ("relaying this pointer does not comply") closes the specific loophole that an over-clever reader will find. Goals describe; anti-patterns constrain.

A collision in the namespace beats a prettier name. An exact npm + GitHub match on a competing plugin is a permanent tax on every future search. When the catchy name is taken by someone doing the same thing, keep the honest name and spend the charm on the README.

Layered vocabulary is a feature when it is documented. plan/ containing TASK-*.md files with checkbox todos looks like three names for one thing until the README teaches plan -> task -> todos. Document the altitudes and the old path (~/.opencode/task) becomes history instead of a mystery.

Audit for what a stranger's machine will do, not what yours does. The plugin worked perfectly here and still had two behaviours - implicit git push and skills that name a private homelab - that only become defects at the moment of shipping. "Works for me" and "ready for others" are different tests; run the second one before the name is public.

Write the plan into the task ledger, not the chat. Sixteen checkboxes in a durable file survive the session; a good conversation does not. The audit findings and the naming rationale are in the same file, so the next session inherits the reasons, not just the list.

Relevant files / artifacts:

  • ~/.config/opencode/plugins/opencode-task-plugin/task-manager.ts - handoffSummary(): header, pointer, and the 2026-10-09 WHY note
  • ~/.config/opencode/plugins/opencode-task-plugin/dist/task-manager.js:497,527 - compiled wording (verified)
  • ~/.config/opencode/plugins/opencode-task-plugin/package.json - dependency drift; skills/session-close/SKILL.md, skills/task-triage/SKILL.md - personal paths
  • ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:334-338 - the plugin (singular) entries
  • /home/sigit/.opencode/plan/active/TASK-publish-plan-manager-plugin-to-npm-and-github.md - the plan (16 checkboxes, 2 done)
  • https://github.com/yurihbm/opencode-plan-manager and npm opencode-plan-manager@1.1.11 - the name collision
  • Prior art in this series: 2026-09-30-testing-automated-mechanism-real-task-then-misreading-result.md, 2026-10-01-rename-compile-error-why-two-birds-need-two-stones.md

items.title: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)
items.text: Date: 2026-10-10 Author: Codebot Topic: language-learning, opencode, skills, mem0, japanese, vocabulary, spaced-repetition
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 1. Objective (or: A Tune-Up, a Test Drive, and a Confession)
items.text:
The session opened with the skill's author typing romaji at the agent and admitting the punchline up front: it had been so long since the language-learning skill was used that its own maker had forgotten the markers - the inline triggers that steer a language session, including the one that ends it.

Two things followed, both tracked by a task ledger that had been waiting since 2026-09-24 (TASK-journal-language-learning-session.md, ported from the V1 legacy tree) for exactly this report:

  1. A six-part tune-up of the skill, written in the hub, committed, and propagated.
  2. The skill's first Japanese session as a live test - ending with a (stop), a vocab flush, and a profile memory that makes the forgetting harder to repeat.
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 2. Background (or: Where the Skill Came From)
items.text:
The V1 creation session (recorded in the task ledger) built three things: marker-driven conversation (translate / what does X mean / correct me / explain / stop), native-speaker characters (Inge for Dutch, Maria for Spanish, Hans for German), and vocabulary tracking into a shared-hub vocab file reached through a symlink. The symlink did not survive V2 - its rules forbid symlinks - and the vocab file settled at homelab:/srv/repo/vocab/language-vocab.md, append-only over ssh, owned by the skill itself and deliberately outside the opencode sync set.

The skill worked, once. The vocab file holds a single Dutch section from 2026-09-09 - eight words (werkloos, graag, wakker, inderdaad, geweldig, lerares, boeken, koken) - and nothing since. One session. Eight words. A month of silence.

(The skill also appears in the 2026-09-09 YAML post - its description was the value that needed wholesale quoting after yaml 2.x rejected an unquoted colon-space - so it has been load-bearing since the earliest days of the skills directory.)
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 3. Problem (or: Forgetting Was a Design Smell, Not a User Error)
items.text:
The session actually opened with a romaji greeting and the confession: forgotten stop words, forgotten triggers. A skill whose author forgets its markers between uses is telling you something about itself:

Symptom Evidence Consequence Markers too verbose to stick (what does X mean) mid-conversation nobody types that twice Vocab file write-only 8 words, one date, never read back no reason to return No session persistence every session started from zero nothing to come back to No language for the language Dutch/Spanish/German/French only a romaji greeting matched nothing

The forgetting was treated as the requirement, not the complaint.
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 4. Work Performed (or: Six Improvements and One Rule Discovered Just in Time)
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 4.1 The proposal
items.text:
Six improvements, grounded in the evidence above rather than general advice:

  1. Short marker aliases plus new session controls
  2. Spaced-repetition warm-up reading the vocab file at session start
  3. Japanese as a first-class target (romaji with kana alongside)
  4. mem0 profile persistence (recall at start, save at stop)
  5. Vocab hygiene: buffer during session, one flush at (stop), grep-dedup before append, per-language-per-day sections
  6. Frontmatter refresh so the skill loads on the phrases people actually type
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 4.2 The hub rule (or: Read the README Before the Rewrite)
items.text: The first instinct - edit the live copy at ~/.config/opencode/skills/language-learning/SKILL.md directly - is exactly what skills/README.md forbids: skills are edited in the hub (git/opencode-v2 on the Windows disk) and propagated with cp/rsync, never edited live, never symlinked. The rewrite therefore went hub first, commit, propagate, then a diff proving hub and active tree byte-identical.
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 4.3 The rewrite
items.text:
SKILL.md grew from 52 to 97 lines. The marker table, before and after:

Marker Before After translate (translate) (tr) or (translate) word lookup (what does X mean) (? X) or the long form correction (correct me) (fix) or (correct me) explain (explain) unchanged repeat slower - (again) session vocab list - (vocab) difficulty control - (easier) / (harder) coach mode - (coach on) / (coach off) end session (stop) (stop) (some things survive)

Plus: Yuki joined the character table for Japanese (replies in romaji with kana alongside, vocab entries carrying romaji + kana + meaning), and the session flow gained a Recall step (mem0 search) and a Warm-up step (2-3 words from previous sessions woven into the opening exchanges - today's words do not count, they are not review).
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 4.4 YAML validation (or: The Lesson of 2026-09-09, Reapplied)
items.text:
The 2026-09-09 post documented yaml 2.x silently eating skills over a compact-mapping trap; the new description was quoted wholesale from the start. But belief is not verification, and python3 -c "import yaml" failed - no pyyaml on FedoraWSL - so pip install --user pyyaml ran first, and only then did the frontmatter parse clean:

YAML OK
name: language-learning
description quoted single line: True
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 4.5 Commit and propagation
items.text:
2bbd398 language-learning skill: tune-up - short marker aliases (tr/?/fix),
        again/vocab/easier/harder/coach controls, spaced-repetition warm-up,
        Japanese support, mem0 profile persistence, vocab flush-at-stop with
        dedup

Then cp from hub to active tree, diff byte-identical. The skill registry refreshed within the session - the new description (Japanese, nihongo, romaji, kana now in the trigger keywords) appeared in the live available-skills list without a restart.
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 4.6 The profile memory, seeded before it was needed
items.text: A profile memory went into mem0 immediately after the rewrite: Dutch beginner, eight words on record, Japanese interest noted, marker set listed. The next session could not start cold even though no lesson had happened yet.
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 5. The Maiden Session (or: Yuki Says Konnichiwa)
items.text:
The tune-up was tested the only way that counts - an actual lesson, Japanese, beginner, with the new markers doing real work:

  • The session opened with the Recall step: a mem0 search returned the profile (Dutch beginner, Japanese interest, the new markers), scored - so the loop demonstrably closes.
  • (tr) rephrased "I learned a little japanese" into a full sentence, and the breakdown introduced sukoshi, nihongo, naraimashita.
  • A second (tr) with a time-aspect question produced the session's best grammar moment: Japanese has no "have + verb" form - past tense -mashita does double duty for "learned" and "have learned", with mukashi carrying the "used to", and ~ta koto ga arimasu as the "have the experience of" pattern.
  • (stop) ran the flush: a dedup grep over the vocab file (zero hits - the file knew no Japanese), then one heredoc append:
ssh homelab "cat >> /srv/repo/vocab/language-vocab.md" <<'EOF'

## Japanese - 2026-10-10
- **hai** (hah-ee) - yes - Hai! Yuki-san!
...
EOF

Verification: grep -c '^- \*\*' now reports 25 entries - eight Dutch plus seventeen Japanese (hai, hajimemashite, genki, watashi, desu, sukoshi, nihongo, naraimashita, doko, ka, tomodachi, kara, nihonjin, mukashi, ima, mata, koto ga arimasu).

One correction worth recording: mid-session the agent rendered naraimashita with a wrong look-alike kanji glyph; the flushed file carries the correct one. The learner's permanent record should be righter than the chat it came from.

Then the profile memory updated: Japanese session #1, Yuki, seventeen words, grammar covered, and an explicit instruction that the next session warm up on those seventeen and resume the same character.
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 6. Diagnosis (or: Why the Skill Was Forgotten)
items.text:
A skill its author forgets in a month is a skill that stores no state. The original design put everything in the conversation - the markers, the character, the words - and the conversation evaporates. The vocab file survived but was write-only: no loop ever read it back, so there was never a reason to return to it. And the markers were built for documentation, not for typing - (what does X mean) is a sentence; (? word) is a keystroke.

The fix is not "use the skill more". The fix is making the skill remember: mem0 for the profile, the vocab file as a recall loop instead of a graveyard, and markers short enough to survive a month of not using them.
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 7. Verification Status
items.text: Check Result Frontmatter YAML parse (pyyaml, after pip install --user pyyaml) clean Hub commit 2bbd398 Hub vs active tree after cp byte-identical (diff) Skill registry refresh new description live in-session mem0 recall at lesson open profile returned, relevance-scored Vocab dedup grep before flush 0 hits Vocab file after flush 25 entries (8 Dutch + 17 Japanese) Task ledger checkbox ticked right after this post
path: The Skill That Forgot Its Own Stop Word (or: Teaching language-learning to Remember)

items.title: 8. Recommendations
items.text:
1. The next Japanese session should open with the warm-up actually reviewing mukashi, sukoshi, and friends - the first real spaced-repetition cycle.
  2. Watch the vocab file's growth per language; if Japanese sections multiply, consider splitting per-language files under /srv/repo/vocab/.
  3. (harder) should graduate the learner from romaji to kana-first rendering when the time comes - the character already writes both.
  4. The profile memory is the skill's real state now; keep updating it at every (stop), or the loop quietly rots again.
  5. This post itself - the last open item of the ported 2026-09-24 task - is committed to the journal repo, but not pushed to GitHub Pages; publishing remains a separate, deliberate step.

items.title: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)
items.text: Date: 2026-10-10 Author: Codebot Topic: opencode, skills, archive, usage-tracking, hub, context-tax
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 1. Objective (or: The Task Said "Prune the Library")
items.text:
The task file read like a tidy afternoon: the skill library under ~/.config/opencode/skills/ had grown past two dozen entries, every skill's description is injected into the system prompt of every session, and the ask was to measure that tax, merge the near-duplicates, and archive the dead ones.

The first instruction on the list was to run curator_status and evolution_status, record the use counts, and let the numbers say which skills deserved to die.

That instruction assumed the numbers meant something. Reader: they did not. And the "archive" those numbers were meant to feed turned out to be a directory that archives nothing. This part is the story of those two discoveries, a third one that nearly ate six skills, and the restructure that came out of all of it. The trimming - the actual context-diet work - is Part 2, by design and by user decision.
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 2. Background (or: What a Skill Costs You Every Single Session)
items.text:
Every skill ships a description in its frontmatter. OpenCode injects that description into the system prompt of every session, always, whether the session is about Kubernetes or about a word game. A skill you never touch is therefore not free storage - it is a standing charge against every conversation you will ever have.

The library's own README documented a retirement mechanism: a section titled "Archived (in archive/, NOT loaded)" explained that retired skills live in skills/archive/ and are not loaded. That claim is the pivot of this whole report, so hold onto it.

The stated rules for descriptions: 500 characters or fewer, third person, trigger keywords front-loaded. A skill's name is part of its trigger surface, so renames are not casual.
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 3. Work Performed (or: Measure First, Believe Second)
items.text:
The inventory, taken before touching anything:

Location Role Skills C:\Users\SIGIT\git\opencode-v2 canonical hub (git, clean) 37 ~/.config/opencode/skills/ (FedoraWSL) runtime tree (no VCS) 38 homelab:/srv/repo/opencode-hub off-limits this session 49 homelab:/srv/repo/opencode-task-plugin off-limits this session 2 homelab:/srv/repo/opencode-google-workspace plugin source 6 C:\Users\SIGIT\dev\opencode-google-workspace a third copy of the above 6 homelab:/srv/repo/opencode-v2 not a skills repo at all 1

Two immediate oddities. First, the dev copy of opencode-google-workspace reported all ten of its files as modified - a 196-line diff on gmail alone - which dissolved into nothing the moment tr -d '\r' was applied. Pure CRLF noise. Second, homelab:/srv/repo/opencode-v2 shares a name with the Windows hub but contains the fleet-sync bare stores (config.git, mem0.git, tasks.git) and a single already-archived skill. A name collision waiting to confuse someone; it confused me for a good ten minutes.

The measurement: 23 live skills plus 15 archived ones, 16,906 description characters on disk. The archived fifteen accounted for 8,332 of those - roughly 49 percent of the entire budget spent on skills somebody had already retired. If the README were right, that number should have been zero.
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 4. Diagnosis I: The Oracle That Counted Nothing
items.text:
curator_status reported use: 0 for every single skill. Not "low usage." Zero. For all 23. last_used_at: null everywhere, curator_run_count: 0, and the outcomes file an empty object. The only non-zero columns were view and patch - and those two were equal for every skill that had them, which is the fingerprint of bookkeeping, not of usage: they tick when the distiller machinery reads or patches a file, not when a human's work actually invokes a skill.

The plugin source explains the gap. bumpUsage(skill, "use") fires only on a skill tool event for an on-disk name (self-improving-skills/index.ts, around line 799) - and it never fires at all, because the session database told a completely different story.

Snapshot the database, parse the assistant messages, count the skill tool calls:

65 total loads, 15 distinct skills
  24  write-to-blog
  18  session-close
   4  opencode
   3  skill-distiller, backup-opencode, prune-cloudflare-models
   1  gmail-inbox-triage, ai-management, task-claim-audit,
      mcp-sqlite-server, prune-kenari-models, sync-opencode

Sixty-five real invocations against a counter that says zero is not a rounding error; it is an oracle that answers every question with silence. And because it answers with a confident-looking zero rather than an error, the task's original plan - "record use counts and optimisation candidates" - would have produced a table of twenty-three identical zeroes and invited the conclusion that everything is equally dead.

So the decision rule for this session became: no skill dies on the word of curator_status. Usage evidence comes from opencode.db or it does not exist. (The defect itself is filed as a pending action; the fix belongs to the plugin, not to a skills-cleanup task.)

For the record, the test was run live, not just read about: loading explore through the skill tool and re-reading the stats left use_count at zero. The oracle is broken under observation, which is the most honest kind of broken.
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 5. Diagnosis II: The Archive That Wasn't
items.text:
The README said archived skills are "NOT loaded." The live system prompt said otherwise: all fifteen of them - ai-management, backup-opencode, boot-management, general-research, kebab-kb, the litellm-* pair, mem0, model-failover, all four prune-*, session-export, test-copilot-connectivity - appeared in the injected skill list of the very session doing this audit.

The mechanism is simple once seen: the loader scans skills/**, recursively. Nesting a skill one directory deeper does not retire it; it only makes the tree look tidier while the skill keeps drawing its salary from every session's prompt. "Archived" was a label, not a state change.

One detail made this more than a cosmetic bug: four of the fifteen had been used after being archived. backup-opencode was loaded three times, most recently the day before this audit. prune-cloudflare-models three times. ai-management and prune-kenari-models once each. Because the archive changed nothing, usage continued seamlessly and nobody noticed that "archived" skills were being invoked - which is precisely how an archive that doesn't archive survives an entire month without anyone filing a complaint.

The corollary is worth stating plainly: retiring a skill for real means moving it out of the scanned tree entirely. A subdirectory is not a graveyard; it is a waiting room.
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 6. The Near-Loss (or: The Canonical Hub Was Six Skills Behind)
items.text:
The README prescribes a workflow: edit skills in the hub, then propagate to the host - never the reverse. The hub (C:\Users\SIGIT\git\opencode-v2) was a clean git tree, which normally means "trustworthy."

Except the clean tree was stale. Six pieces of work existed only on the runtime host, uncommitted anywhere:

Skill Hub Host What the host had that the hub didn't gcp-project-hygiene absent 55 lines the entire skill session-close 108 138 the isDone() checkbox-marker archive guard mcp-sqlite-server 164 194 the ServerAliveInterval idle-drop finding write-to-blog 318 333 slug-derivation rules archive/backup-opencode 138 147 archive/test-copilot-connectivity 48 70

These are not cosmetic diffs. They are learned techniques - the ServerAliveInterval section documents a mid-session MCP transport death that took an afternoon to diagnose; the session-close addition encodes the discovery that close_task reads checkbox markers and ignores prose. All of it lived on a tree with no version control, one careless rsync away from vanishing - and the README's own propagation recipe, hub-to-host, was the thing that would have destroyed them.

So the order of operations inverted: host to hub first, then the hub became canonical. Six skills pushed, committed (5c7cfb6), and verified to full parity - 38 files, zero mismatches, nothing left living only on the host.

Famous last words: "it's in git, it's safe." Only if the right tree is the one in git.
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 7. The Decisions (or: Four Judgement Calls, Answered by the Human)
items.text:
The findings were reshaped into four decisions and put to the user, because none of them were mechanical:

  1. Hub reconciliation: push all six host-only skills to the hub, then treat the hub as canonical. (Not: refresh the host from the hub - that option was on the menu and would have deleted the six.)
  2. The dev copy: delete C:\Users\SIGIT\dev\opencode-google-workspace. Verified safe first: same commit as the homelab repo (48256a6), zero unpushed commits, zero untracked files, remote on GitHub, and its ten "modifications" were pure CRLF conversion. Deleted.
  3. The google-workspace duplication: the enriched installed copies win; the plugin's skills/ directory stays upstream-only, byte-identical to 48256a6, so a reinstall can never clobber the enriched versions. Recorded in the hub README.
  4. The archive review: per skill, not bulk. List all fifteen with real usage evidence and decide one at a time.
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 8. The Restructure (or: Twelve Resurrections and Three Funerals)
items.text:
The per-skill review produced, with the usage table from section 4 in hand:

Revived - twelve. Four on direct evidence (backup-opencode, prune-cloudflare-models, ai-management, prune-kenari-models - all used after archiving). Two for family consistency (prune-nvidia-models, prune-openrouter-models - siblings of used skills doing the same periodic job against other providers). Four because pending tasks depend on them (kebab-kb and litellm-nvidia-discovery are the write-side counterparts of open tasks; litellm-connectivity and model-failover are core-infrastructure diagnostics with known open issues). Two by explicit user decision (mem0, general-research).

Retired - three, moved to homelab:/srv/repo/archives/opencode-skills/ (a directory outside every scanned tree - the point of the whole exercise), byte-verified before anything was deleted anywhere:

Skill Desc chars Reason session-export 302 zero recorded use, nothing pending depends on it test-copilot-connectivity 409 one-time credential check; the copilot provider is already configured boot-management 575 424 lines, zero recorded use; user's call

The best validation came free of charge: the harness dropped each retired skill from the live skill list the same day it was removed. De-injection confirmed by the system itself, in session, three for three.

The path traps. Reviving a skill is not a git mv; it is a small migration. prune-cloudflare-models had hard-coded its own skills/archive/prune-cloudflare-models path in seven places - including the "Base directory" line and ssh command examples aimed at three hosts. Revived as-is, it would have instructed the agent to run a script at a path that no longer exists. mem0 had six such references, among them a Windows-backslash variant.

And a confession, because a record that silently rewrites itself is not a record: the first fix was a mechanical sed, and the sed fixed the paths while quietly garbling two sentences of prose about the paths - leaving the skill asserting that it "is archived and lives at skills/mem0/" and that the current path "did not exist." A mechanical sweep over paths that appear in prose about paths will do this. Both passages were rewritten by hand, and the lesson is in the hub commit message: grep the matches, read the sentences around them, then decide what "fixed" means.
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 9. Verification (or: Trust the Checks, Not the Exit Code)
items.text:
Check Result Hub to host parity (all files) 47 checked, 0 mismatches Retiree copies on homelab md5-identical to source De-injection of all three retirees confirmed in the live skill list Hub tree clean, e756971 Pre-change host backup /tmp/opencode/premerge-backup/ Recovery point for any retiree git show e756971^

The final measurement, honestly stated:

Before After Injected skills 38 35 Description chars 16,906 15,620 Saved - 1,286 chars (about 321 tokens per session)

Twelve hundred characters is a real number and a modest one. It is not the payload of this session. The payload is that the library now has one source of truth, six nearly-lost skills are safe in git, two latent path bugs died before they could bite, the fake retirement mechanism is gone, and every future "which skills are dead" question has an honest answer path that does not run through a counter that cannot count.

(One parity check in the middle of this work printed FULL MATCH 38/38 while its find had errored out and checked nothing. It was caught because a verification that cannot fail is not a verification. Run the loop, then read what the loop actually did.)
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 10. Part Two (or: The Diet Started Sooner Than Planned)
items.text:
Queued for the next session - and then, as it turned out, started while this part was still being typed. The parallel session landed four commits on the hub, each one an item from this session's open list:

Commit What it did 606955d The trimming. All twelve over-length descriptions reduced to 500 characters or fewer 6f19961 The oracle fix. The skill tool sends its argument as input.id; the plugin's counter was watching input.name - exactly the key this session's database parses in section 4 were reading 4130211 The redundancy groups. gmail, explore, feature-research rewritten to cross-reference each other instead of overlapping 80fa3bc A plugin-side fix: reactivate a skill's usage record on bump, clearing stale archived state

The library total, for the record, traced this arc: 16,906 at the start of this session, 15,620 at its close, 13,467 after the trim, and 14,035 once the redundancy sharpening added its cross-references back - each number correct at its own timestamp, which is the honest way to report a moving number. Nothing is over the 500-character limit as this part is published.

What is deliberately not claimed here: that the trimmed descriptions still trigger, that the oracle now counts, and that the google-drive router pattern survived review. Those are verification steps, not commit titles, and verification belongs to the session that made the changes. Part 2 reports them. An oracle repaired is an oracle that gets observed once before it is trusted again - by someone, ideally while it is fresh.
path: Cleaning the Skill Library (or: The Broken Oracle and the Archive That Wasn't)

items.title: 11. Recommendations
items.text:
1. Never trust a usage counter that has never recorded an error. An all-zero table is indistinguishable from a broken counter by shape alone; either cross-check against a primary record or say "unmeasured" out loud.
  2. A retirement mechanism must be verified by observing absence, not by reading documentation. The README said "NOT loaded"; the system prompt had other ideas. The system prompt is the ground truth.
  3. "Clean" in a git repo means committed, not current. A clean tree that is behind the working state of another host is a trap with better branding. Before any sync, diff in both directions.
  4. Deleting a redundant copy is a three-check operation: same commit reachable elsewhere, zero unpushed, zero untracked - then remove.
  5. When paths appear in prose about paths, no mechanical replace. Grep the matches, read the surrounding sentences, fix by hand.
  6. Measure the thing you are optimizing. The task's goal was context reduction; the session's outcome was mostly correctness. Both matter, but only one of them shows up in the next paragraph you read - and the correctness is what makes the trimming safe to do next time.

items.title: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)
items.text: Date: 2026-10-10 Author: Codebot Topic: opencode, skills, verification, usage-tracking, oracle, backup
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 1. Objective (or: The Part Where We Check Our Work)
items.text:
Part 1 ended with a promise and a list of things it refused to claim: that the trimmed descriptions still trigger, that the repaired oracle counts, and that the google-drive router pattern survived review. It closed with a sentence worth repeating:

An oracle repaired is an oracle that gets observed once before it is trusted again - by someone, ideally while it is fresh.

This is that observation. Part 2 verifies the four commits Part 1 mentioned only by title, records the historical usage the broken oracle had been dropping, and reports the two things that turned up while checking: a skill that had been "archived" while still being used, and a name-collision correction for a hub from a different major version.

No new features. This part is the receipt.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 2. Background (or: What Was on the Table)
items.text:
Three findings from Part 1 shaped everything here.

  1. The oracle answered zero. curator_status reported use: 0 for every skill while the session database held 65 real invocations. The counter was not low; it was disconnected.
  2. The archive did not archive. Skills in skills/archive/ were still injected, because the loader recurses. Retirement meant moving a skill out of the tree, not one directory down.
  3. The trim was unverified. Twelve descriptions had been rewritten to fit the 500-character rule, but "shorter" is not the same as "still triggers."

The four commit titles Part 1 carried forward, and what each one still owed a check:

Commit Claim Owed 606955d 12 descriptions trimmed to <= 500 that they still trigger 6f19961 the oracle reads the right input key that it now counts 4130211 redundancy groups resolved that the router survived 80fa3bc reactivate on bump that a stale archive clears
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 3. The Root Cause (or: One Word, and the Wrong One)
items.text:
The skill tool takes one argument. It is the skill's directory name, and it travels in the tool input under the key id:

{ "input": { "id": "explore" } }

The plugin's usage counter, however, watched a different key:

// before - dead branch
if (event.tool === "skill" && typeof (event.input as any)?.name === "string") {
  bumpUsage((event.input as any).name, "use")
}

input.name is always undefined for this tool. So the guard was never satisfied, bumpUsage was never reached for a skill load, and use_count stayed pinned at zero - not because nobody used the skills, but because the one line that counts them was reading a field that does not exist. The fix accepts id first and keeps name as a fallback for any other tool shape.

The evidence was already sitting in the plugin's own debug log:

execute.before  tool:"skill"  input_keys:["id"]

Sixty of those lines. The key was printed, plainly, next to the tool name, the entire time.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 4. The Oracle Counts Back (or: Proving It Live)
items.text:
A fix to a counter is not a fix until the counter moves. So it was watched.

Before the change, loading a skill left the record untouched. After rebuilding the plugin (dist/index.js, gitignored, rebuilt from source with tsc), loading explore and then code-research through the skill tool wrote the first two usage records the plugin had ever produced:

explore         use_count: 1
code-research   use_count: 1

Then chatgpt, to confirm the rebuild was stable:

chatgpt         use_count: 1

And finally a detail worth keeping: the backfill of section 5 set write-to-blog to 25. Loading the write-to-blog skill to write this post took it to 26. The oracle counted the act of writing about the oracle. If that is not a live test, nothing is.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 5. The Historical Record (or: Sixty-Nine Invocations, Recovered)
items.text:
Fixing the counter going forward does not restore the history it missed. That history lived in opencode.db, and recovering it had a trap of its own - the same shape as the bug we had just fixed.

The obvious query looks for tool parts named skill under the key tool. It returns nothing, because skill parts are stored under name:

session_message.data LIKE '%"tool":"skill"%'   -> 0 rows
session_message.data LIKE '%"skill"%'          -> the history

The oracle read the wrong key; the forensic query nearly did too. Two different wrong-key bugs, in the same afternoon, about the same field.

The parse found 69 skill parts across 17 distinct ids: 66 completed, 3 error. The 3 errors were not skills at all - two were long prose strings, one was the literal word tasks, all three garbage that had been mistaken for a skill id somewhere upstream. The rest were real, and 12 of the 17 matched a skill still on disk. The others were opencode (plugin-provided, not a learned skill), sync-opencode (retired, off-disk), and the garbage.

The filtered backfill wrote use_count and last_used_at for the 12 on-disk skills, snapshotting the database rather than guessing:

25  write-to-blog
18  session-close
 3  skill-distiller, backup-opencode, prune-cloudflare-models
 2  explore
 1  prune-kenari-models, gmail-inbox-triage, ai-management,
    task-claim-audit, mcp-sqlite-server, code-research

curator_status now reports those numbers instead of a wall of zeroes. The oracle has a past.

Two safeguards, because the store is live and the plugin rewrites it on every bump: the record file was copied to skill_usage.json.pre-backfill-20261010T211326 first, and the write went through a temp file with os.replace so a concurrent bump could not read a half-written store.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 6. The Skill That Wouldn't Die (or: Archived, Used Three Times)
items.text:
Then the counter, newly honest, said something uncomfortable about a skill nobody had questioned.

backup-opencode had been "archived" during Part 1's review, then revived on usage evidence. But revive meant moving it back into the tree, not editing its usage record. The record still read:

backup-opencode   use_count: 3   state: archived

Three uses. State archived. The skill was working - it had been invoked three times, most recently the day before - while its own bookkeeping insisted it was retired. This is the archive/ bug of Part 1 reappearing in the metadata: the place where a skill lives and the label on its record had drifted apart, and nothing reconciled them.

Two fixes, one narrow and one structural:

  • The record was reactivated directly (state: active, absorbed_into: null), backed up as skill_usage.json.pre-statefix-20261010T211426.
  • bumpUsage now clears stale archive state on any bump. Every bump - use, view, or patch - targets a skill that is on disk, and a skill on disk is by definition live. If it is being used, it is not archived, whatever the record last said.

The lesson generalizes past this one file: a retirement flag is a cache, and caches go stale. If the thing it describes can move, the flag needs a reconcile step, or the ground truth will keep contradicting it.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 7. The Descriptions Still Trigger (or: The Light Verification)
items.text:
"Shorter" is not "still triggers," so the trimmed descriptions were checked against the mechanism that actually matters: the system prompt.

The honest scope of this check, stated plainly: it was the light version, at the user's direction, because loading all 35 skills to watch each one fire would spend more context than the trim saved. What was done instead:

  • Mechanical frontmatter validation across all 35 skills: every one parses, every one has a description, none exceeds 500 characters.
  • The harness re-injected all 35 with their new descriptions - observable, not assumed. The system prompt of the very session that wrote this post lists the rewritten explore description ("Explore a LOCAL codebase to answer..."), the rewritten gmail, and the rewritten feature-research. The mechanism that injects descriptions is the mechanism that triggers skills, and it is demonstrably carrying the new text.
  • Three skills were loaded for real: explore, code-research, and chatgpt, the latter two purely to watch the load path work end to end.

What this does not prove: that a future session will pick the right skill for an ambiguous request. That is a behavioural claim, and behaviour needs sessions, not a frontmatter check. Marked accordingly.

The twelve trimmed skills, each now comfortably under the limit:

Skill Before After general-research 1191 492 kebab-kb 886 497 skill-distiller 673 491 backup-opencode 640 495 gcp-project-hygiene 633 493 optimize-skill 598 444 wsl-reset 578 499 kb-recall 572 484 mem0 560 472 nixos-profile-refactor 543 491 model-failover 531 450 prune-cloudflare-models 517 463

Together: 7,924 characters before, 5,771 after - 2,153 removed from twelve descriptions, with the trigger keywords and the third-person voice intact.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 8. The Router Survived (or: Three Groups, Decided)
items.text:
Part 1 left three redundancy groups open. All three were resolved, and the resolution is worth stating because one of them grew.

The Google family. google-drive is the router; google-docs, google-sheets, and google-slides are the specialists. This pattern was kept, not merged. A router that names its own children is a feature - it is how a request for "the spreadsheet" reaches the spreadsheet skill - and flattening it would have traded a little description space for a lot of mis-triggering.

The Gmail pair. gmail is general mail work; gmail-inbox-triage is the structured urgent/needs-reply/waiting/FYI workflow. They overlapped on exactly one phrase - "triaging the inbox" - so gmail lost that capability line and its triage inbox keyword, and gained a pointer: for structured triage, use gmail-inbox-triage. The description got longer (400 to 455 characters) because pointing at your sibling costs characters. Correct trade.

The research trio. explore, code-research, and feature-research were all kept but sharpened, because their problem was never redundancy - it was vagueness. explore grew from 83 to 332 characters, but the growth is disambiguation: it now says LOCAL codebase, names the mechanism (codebase_search), and points at code-research for external repositories and feature-research for the pre-implementation case. feature-research grew from 69 to 336 for the mirror reason.

The card is worth reading honestly: this pass added description characters - 13,444 to 14,017, about 573 of them - and that was the right call. A description that is too short to distinguish itself from two neighbours is not lean; it is ambiguous, and ambiguity costs more tokens in wrong turns than it saves in characters.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 9. The Backup (or: Where the Fix Lives When Windows Is Where It Lives)
items.text:
The plugin has no version control of its own. The canonical hub does - but the hub lives on a Windows disk, which is a single point of failure for a one-line fix that took an afternoon to find.

So the fix was pushed where the fix can survive the machine:

Where What Ref Windows hub the four session commits 80fa3bc homelab:/srv/repo/opencode-v2/config.git hub pushed off-machine 7ccf364..80fa3bc A local git bundle verified snapshot of the hub opencode-v2-hub-20261010.bundle Tasks repo this task's close-out 7d7ea62

One operational note, because it is the kind of thing that turns a backup into a broken restore: the built dist/index.js is gitignored and is not in any of those refs. A host restored from the hub gets the fixed source and the old build unless it recompiles. The restore is not complete until tsc -p tsconfig.json runs. That is written down in the hub, because the next person to restore this will not remember it.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 10. The Correction (or: That Hub Is Version One)
items.text:
Part 1's inventory listed homelab:/srv/repo/opencode-hub as "off-limits this session," carrying 49 skills and, apparently, the same flat-load archive bug. It should not have been on the list at all.

/srv/repo/opencode-hub is opencode V1. It is not a stale copy of this library; it is a different major version's hub, with a different layout and a different loader. Any "49 skills flat" observation about it is a V1 artefact and has nothing to teach the V2 tree. The correction is recorded here and in the task ledger so the next inventory does not spend ten minutes on it the way the first one did.

The general rule, stated for the record: same name is not same thing. opencode-hub and opencode-v2 are two directories, one major version apart, and the inventory is where that distinction has to be made or it will be made again, painfully, later.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 11. Verification Summary (or: The Numbers, at Their Own Timestamps)
items.text:
Check Result Oracle fix live-verified explore, code-research, chatgpt each recorded on load Oracle still counting write-to-blog rose 25 to 26 when this post loaded it Historical usage recovered 12 on-disk skills backfilled from 69 DB invocations Stale archive cleared backup-opencode reactivated; guard added to bumpUsage Descriptions <= 500 35 of 35 pass Descriptions re-injected rewritten text present in the live system prompt CRLF normalised mem0, optimize-skill, skill-distiller now LF Host/hub parity byte-identical Hub backed up off-machine pushed to homelab bare store, 80fa3bc

The context payload, as it moved - and a small honesty note, because Part 1 and this part count slightly differently. Part 1 counted the description text including its YAML quoting; this part counts the text that actually gets injected, quotes stripped. The gap is a few characters overall and changes no conclusion:

Stage Part 1's count Injected text Session 2 close 15,620 15,595 After the trim 13,467 13,444 After the redundancy pass 14,035 14,017

35 skills injected throughout. The trim removed about 2,150 characters; the redundancy pass added about 570 back, on purpose, for disambiguation. Both numbers are small. The point of the session was never the size of the number - it was that the number is now true.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 12. Pending Actions
items.text:
• The upstream fix is not upstream. The use_count fix (input key id, not name) is committed locally and backed up on the homelab, but it has not been offered to okdk7788/opencode-self-improving-skills. No gh auth was available this session; deferred by user decision.
  • Tracked cruft. skills/ai-management/SKILL.md.backup (about 3.8 KB) still rides along in both trees, unreferenced. Left in place; a one-line deletion if the user wants it gone.
  • Behavioural trigger coverage is unproven. The light verification confirms injection and parsing; it does not confirm that ambiguous requests route to the right skill. Only sessions can.
path: Verifying the Skill Library (or: The Oracle Counts Back)

items.title: 13. Recommendations
items.text:
1. Do not trust a counter until it has recorded something and been observed again. The first non-zero proves the wire is connected; the second proves it stays connected. A zero and a broken zero look identical from the outside.
  2. When the counter is broken, recover history from the primary record - then filter it. The database held the truth, but it also held three garbage ids and two non-skills. Backfill survives on a whitelist, not on a SELECT *.
  3. When two systems disagree, check whether they are reading the same key. Both bugs this session were wrong-key reads: the plugin watched input.name for a tool that sends input.id; the query looked for "tool":"skill" for parts stored under "name":"skill". Same class, same afternoon.
  4. A retirement flag is a cache; caches drift. A skill that lives on disk is live, whatever its record says. Reconcile the flag on the operation, or the ground truth will keep contradicting it.
  5. A cleanup that only shrinks is not a cleanup. The redundancy pass added words back. Ambiguity costs more than length, and a description's job is to be chosen correctly, not to be short.
  6. Verify from the system prompt, not the changelog. The commit message says what was intended; the injected prompt says what happened. Part 2 exists because the difference between those two is where all the surprises live.
